mitigation_mechanism: Flood peak and flood stage are different outcomes and this evidence moves them in different directions. Roughening and re-wetting the surface — re-vegetating bare peat, blocking gullies, lowering banks so water spreads onto a floodplain — slows storm-water delivery and cuts the discharge peak measured at or just below the works: 27% at a re-vegetated micro-catchment and 51% where gully blocking was added, against a bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N); 49% at a rewetted peat gully (ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow); about 8% to 12% for a base-case modelled floodplain reconnection (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2). The loss frame agrees: bare peat gave higher peaks per unit rainfall (ev_wetflA_acre_barepeat_loss) and embanking a floodplain raised the modelled downstream peak by 57% (ev_wetflA_acre_cherwell_embankment). Stage is the other half of the story — the same floodplain roughness that trims the downstream peak can double the size and depth of the inundated area for a flood of the same size (ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up) — and timing is a third thing again: the gully whose peak fell by 49% also responded faster, its lag between rainfall and peak discharge shortening (ev_wetflA_gatis_lag_reversal).
caveats: Catchment scale and extreme events are the unproven part. No effect was found at the scale of the entire 260 km2 catchment in the best-monitored UK test (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null); the influence of drain blocking on flood flows has been notoriously difficult to detect at basin scale (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null); monitoring cannot isolate a restoration effect from catchment storm-flow data at all (ev_wetflA_shut_catchment_undetectable); and the evidence does not suggest a major difference to downstream flood risk at large catchment scales, or for the most extreme events (ev_wetflA_dads_largecatchment_null, ev_wetflA_dads_summary_extreme_null). During major catastrophic floods the whole basin may be saturated and the presence, absence or management of wetlands has no effect (ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null). The sign also flips with position: an on-site storage gain can still produce an increase in flood peaks at catchment scale through flood-wave synchrony (ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment); a moorland scheme designed to delay runoff partially synchronised sub-catchment peaks and so increased downstream flood risk (ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal); restoring the wrong reach worsened inundation upstream through backwater effects and in some scenarios raised aggregate flood damages above the no-restoration baseline (ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4); and moving the same project downstream along the channel turned a 14% peak reduction into about a 1% increase (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_4). Rewetting also consumes flood storage: raising ditch water levels to meet winter ecological targets cost flood-water storage equivalent to 3% of the median annual flood volume (ev_wetflA_acre_somerset_rewet_cost) — the empty space a flood would fill is exactly what an ecological water-level target removes. Provenance: this is a temperate, high-income corpus, UK and US catchments almost without exception, with no measured low-income or lower-middle-income result in scope; and the benefit is off the farm, arriving at downstream receptors rather than on the plot.

justification.mechanism: Flood peak and flood stage are different outcomes and this evidence moves them in different directions. Roughening and re-wetting the surface — re-vegetating bare peat, blocking gullies, lowering banks so water spreads onto a floodplain — slows storm-water delivery and cuts the discharge peak measured at or just below the works: 27% at a re-vegetated micro-catchment and 51% where gully blocking was added, against a bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N); 49% at a rewetted peat gully (ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow); about 8% to 12% for a base-case modelled floodplain reconnection (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2). The loss frame agrees: bare peat gave higher peaks per unit rainfall (ev_wetflA_acre_barepeat_loss) and embanking a floodplain raised the modelled downstream peak by 57% (ev_wetflA_acre_cherwell_embankment). Stage is the other half of the story — the same floodplain roughness that trims the downstream peak can double the size and depth of the inundated area for a flood of the same size (ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up) — and timing is a third thing again: the gully whose peak fell by 49% also responded faster, its lag between rainfall and peak discharge shortening (ev_wetflA_gatis_lag_reversal).
justification.conditionality: Catchment scale and extreme events are the unproven part. No effect was found at the scale of the entire 260 km2 catchment in the best-monitored UK test (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null); the influence of drain blocking on flood flows has been notoriously difficult to detect at basin scale (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null); monitoring cannot isolate a restoration effect from catchment storm-flow data at all (ev_wetflA_shut_catchment_undetectable); and the evidence does not suggest a major difference to downstream flood risk at large catchment scales, or for the most extreme events (ev_wetflA_dads_largecatchment_null, ev_wetflA_dads_summary_extreme_null). During major catastrophic floods the whole basin may be saturated and the presence, absence or management of wetlands has no effect (ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null). The sign also flips with position: an on-site storage gain can still produce an increase in flood peaks at catchment scale through flood-wave synchrony (ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment); a moorland scheme designed to delay runoff partially synchronised sub-catchment peaks and so increased downstream flood risk (ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal); restoring the wrong reach worsened inundation upstream through backwater effects and in some scenarios raised aggregate flood damages above the no-restoration baseline (ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4); and moving the same project downstream along the channel turned a 14% peak reduction into about a 1% increase (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_4). Rewetting also consumes flood storage: raising ditch water levels to meet winter ecological targets cost flood-water storage equivalent to 3% of the median annual flood volume (ev_wetflA_acre_somerset_rewet_cost) — the empty space a flood would fill is exactly what an ecological water-level target removes. Provenance: this is a temperate, high-income corpus, UK and US catchments almost without exception, with no measured low-income or lower-middle-income result in scope; and the benefit is off the farm, arriving at downstream receptors rather than on the plot.

mitigation_mechanism: Salt marsh dissipates wave energy and takes height off a surge as it travels across the platform. Wave heights fall by 72% across salt marsh, with a 95% confidence interval of 62 to 79% in a meta-analysis of field measurements (ev_flood_hazard_nara16_1); up to 82% of wave energy is dissipated over marsh against 29% over the adjacent sand flat (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_3); storm-surge attenuation rates run from 1.7 to 25 cm per kilometre of marsh depending on marsh and storm characteristics (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_1). The vegetated-versus-unvegetated contrast is consistent — salt marsh vegetation had a significant positive effect on wave attenuation, and every paired study comparing vegetated marsh with intertidal mudflat concluded attenuation is greater over the marsh (ev_flood_hazard_shep11_1, ev_flood_hazard_shep11_2).
caveats: What has been measured is wave attenuation under ordinary conditions: the meta-analysed measurements are all taken under normal conditions of low waves (ev_flood_hazard_nara16_1). The function weakens exactly where protection is wanted — attenuation works less effectively during extreme storms lasting more than a day, which the review reads as a reason not to rely on nature-based flood defences alone in populated low-lying coastal and estuarine areas (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_2). Floodwater attenuation inside the marsh, meaning flood-peak reduction and floodwater storage, has never been quantified: the systematic review found no study evaluating it (ev_flood_hazard_shep11_5). Siting can cancel the benefit, since levees and dikes behind a marsh cause water to set up against the structure and limit the surge-attenuating effect (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_4). The remaining support is self-reported: 41% of salt-marsh projects state that such habitats provide improved protection from storm events (ev_avoided_damage_value_nara16_4). Provenance: existing marsh rather than restored marsh, on high-income US, UK, Dutch, Belgian, Italian and Vietnamese coasts, with coastal property and society as the beneficiary rather than the farm.

mitigation_mechanism: Re-vegetating bare peat and blocking grips and gullies raises surface roughness and storage on the hillslope, so storm water is delivered more slowly. Peak discharge fell 27% at a re-vegetated micro-catchment and 51% where gully blocking was added, both against a bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N), and 49% at a rewetted peat gully (ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow); lag between peak rainfall and peak flow lengthened significantly at the re-vegetated site (ev_wetflA_shut_lag_O), restoration elsewhere produced lower discharge rates observable at drain and hill-stream level, with greater water-table stability and a reduction in peak flows (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_field), and modelling suggests drain blocking in blanket peat could reduce flood flows downstream (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_model). The loss frame points the same way: higher flood peaks and shorter times to peak go with peatland degradation and removal of vegetation cover (ev_wetflA_dads_degradation_loss, ev_wetflA_acre_barepeat_loss). Peak and timing do not behave alike as storms grow — at the gully-blocked site the peak reduction held at 56% in the largest storms while the lag gain collapsed (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_largestorm_N, ev_wetflA_shut_lag_largestorm_N) — and at the rewetted gully the lag shortened even as the peak fell (ev_wetflA_gatis_lag_reversal). Restoration changed the timing and the peak of delivery but not the volume: the runoff coefficient was unchanged at both restored sites (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null).
caveats: The measurements are plot to micro-catchment; the catchment-scale benefit is not demonstrated. No effect was found at the scale of the entire 260 km2 catchment (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null), the influence of drain blocking on flood flows has been notoriously difficult to detect at basin scale (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null), the monitoring authors state that isolating restoration effects within empirical storm-flow datasets is problematic at the large catchment scale (ev_wetflA_shut_catchment_undetectable), and a realistic suite of land-management changes modelled against an extreme rainfall event gave a median flood-peak reduction of only 2% (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_model_2pct). Position decides the sign: upland wetlands tend to be flood-generating areas, frequently saturated with little water storage potential (ev_wetflA_acre_position_upland); blanket bogs close to saturation for most of the year rarely attenuate flow and are much more likely to contribute to storm runoff (ev_wetflA_acre_saturated_bog_reversal); a moorland scheme designed to delay runoff synchronised sub-catchment peaks and increased downstream flood risk (ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal); and an on-site storage gain can still raise peaks at catchment scale (ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment). mitigation_mechanism: Coastal wetland standing between a cyclone and exposed property reduces the damage done, measured as an elasticity across US Atlantic and Gulf coastal counties: a 1% loss of coastal wetlands is associated with a 0.6% increase in property damage (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_1). Built defences substitute for it — the elasticity is 0.50 in states with stricter building codes against 0.81 where codes and enforcement are weaker (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_6). mitigation_mechanism: Drought attacks the restored peat asset through the water table. Across a rewetted Indonesian restoration area and its land-cover types, peat-surface subsidence accelerated sharply during and shortly after the 2019 El Niño drought when groundwater depths were very low, running at 2.5 to 4 times the rate of the preceding 3.5 years and more than double the 7.5-year mean (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_5). Rewetting does not remove the exposure: over the same long record a severe drought could still cause major water-table drops to near 1 m below the peat surface and associated carbon-emission spikes even in otherwise rewetted conditions, in restoration areas and in remaining peat swamp forest alike (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_6).

The second unit is the authors' reading of their own record rather than an independent measurement. What the cell does establish is a project-design implication: a rewetting investment in drought-prone tropical peat should expect the asset to lose surface elevation and carbon in El Niño years regardless of how well the water management performs, and should budget and monitor for that rather than treat it as a failure of the works.

mitigation_mechanism: What wears a salt marsh away is the ordinary wave climate, not the cyclone. A global analysis of salt-marsh erosion and wave measurements found that most salt-marsh deterioration is caused by moderate storms of monthly frequency (ev_erosion_hazard_leon17_6), while intense hurricanes contribute less than 1% to long-term salt-marsh erosion rates (ev_erosion_hazard_leon17_5) — the marsh survives the violent event and is eroded between them.

Provenance is high-income North Atlantic and European coasts.

mitigation_mechanism: The vulnerable asset is the canal dam that holds the water table up. In December 2005, after an extreme rainfall event, both dams in the Kalampangan Canal were damaged by water seeping underneath and along the sides; they were repaired in March 2006 and were damaged again in August 2006 (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_7). caveats: This is a single demonstration site in Indonesian tropical peat, recorded as a case study rather than measured across projects, and the repeat failure after repair is the most transferable part of it. It says nothing about damage to the wetland itself, about coastal or temperate wetland types, or about water-control structures of other designs. Read it as a design and maintenance risk for canal-blocking programmes in deep permeable peat — dam siting relative to the contour, seepage control, and a repair budget that assumes recurrence — rather than as a general sensitivity of wetland management to extreme rainfall. Provenance: humid-tropical, upper-middle-income, with no comparable record from any other peat region.

The rainfall is the trigger; the vulnerability is structural, since highly permeable tropical peat lets seepage pass beneath and alongside a dam, and the sunken canals intercept overland and interflow, raising canal discharges when the rain is extreme.
justification.conditionality: This is a single demonstration site in Indonesian tropical peat, recorded as a case study rather than measured across projects, and the repeat failure after repair is the most transferable part of it. It says nothing about damage to the wetland itself, about coastal or temperate wetland types, or about water-control structures of other designs. Read it as a design and maintenance risk for canal-blocking programmes in deep permeable peat — dam siting relative to the contour, seepage control, and a repair budget that assumes recurrence — rather than as a general sensitivity of wetland management to extreme rainfall. Provenance: humid-tropical, upper-middle-income, with no comparable record from any other peat region.
